Vegetative clearing would be undertaken within a zone 4 feet wide and 8 feet high through the understory along the trail, as well as in the few adjoining public use areas. Some grading may also be required. Although soil movement into streams would occur, this would be minimized through sloping and planting the banks of graded areas and constructing drainage structures as necessary. The trail segment west of Horsepasture River would be steep and could require several switchbacks with appropriate drainage control structures.
3.1.1.2 Scenic and Esthetic Resources
During construction activity, landscape characteristics of the area immediately within the upper reservoir site would change drastically, and the area surrounding the upper reservoir site would change to a lesser degree. In each case the degree of impact would vary towards either extreme depending on visibility. Generally, this impact would be temporary for the duration of construction activities.
The presence in number and type of construction-related equipment would alter what is a beautiful, quiet, and almost wilderness type landscape to one of intensely noisy and dirty activity. What is undeveloped, steeply vegetated topography with several small headwater streams would become large areas involving the clearing of staging areas; a network of access roads; development of spoil and borrow areas; building of a dike, dams, power related facilities; and assorted other excavation activities. A minimum of 820 acres of land would be impacted during construction. About 45 percent of this acreage would be in the reservoir basin and would be ultimately inundated.
The construction of project facilities would not affect the views of motorists extensively, with the only significant exception being the activity involved around the west dam. In this case the significant activity would be the construction of the west dam, the relocation of a short length of South Carolina Highway 171, a new intersection on S.C. 171 to connect with the project access road, and the minor effect of equipment being transported to and from the project site (Figure 3-1). Some of the activities in the upper reservoir area might be visible from South Carolina Route 413 as it approaches from the east (Figure 3-2). These would only be brief glimpses unless one were to stop at one of the several overlook areas for a longer look, which, depending on the viewer, would be relatively insignificant at the distance involved.
